body.text: United States , explained.
The upcoming Xi-Trump meeting on the sidelines of the APEC meeting shouldn’t distract from the fierce AI competition underway.

When Donald Trump and Xi Jinping meet on the sidelines of the APEC summit later this week, AI will be high on the agenda. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has signalled that Washington wants to use the talks to advance a new bilateral dialogue on AI . Yet he also warned that both sides should “harbour no illusions” about their differences – they remain rivals in the race for AI.
However the APEC summit talks go, Washington will need to remain vigilant to stay ahead.

A recent Lowy Institute paper – Asia Power Snapshot: China, the United States, and the race for AI dominance – found that the United States holds a clear lead in the capabilities of its frontier models, driven by its dominance in computing power. To guard that advantage, Washington has sought to limit China’s access to the most advanced technologies. Whatever comes out of the summit, Beijing will continue to seek ways to bypass those restrictions.

Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who recently resigned after admitting to an affair, has renewed attention on Chinese efforts to get around US restrictions. The woman involved is reportedly a former Megaspeed executive. Megaspeed is one of Nvidia’s biggest foreign customers, and according to The New York Times , US officials concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset, a claim Beijing rejects . Megaspeed has faced scrutiny over alleged export violations, which it denies .

Observers have long suspected that smugglers route advanced chips to China through Southeast Asia. In March 2026, US prosecutors charged a co-founder of Super Micro , a server maker, with conspiring to divert servers containing Nvidia chips. Prosecutors alleged that the scheme sent roughly US$2.5 billion worth of AI technology to China. In October 2026, Malaysian customs seized servers containing about US$12 million worth of AI chips at Kuala Lumpur’s international airport.

China has also looked to outsource its computation abroad. The New York Times reported that Megaspeed has used Nvidia chips in data centres across Malaysia and Indonesia that appear to serve China. INF Tech, a Chinese AI startup, has accessed restricted chips by renting them from an Indonesian firm.

Washington has tried to plug some of these gaps. It has pressured Southeast Asian countries such as Malaysia to tighten their regulations , and Congress is advancing legislation to close loopholes. In January 2026, the US House of Representatives passed the Remote Access Security Act , which would extend export controls to cloud-based access to restricted chips. The Senate is yet to vote on it. In March, a House committee passed the Chip Security Act , which would require advanced chips to carry on-chip mechanisms that would verify their location and detect tampering. Complementing these, in May 2026, the US Department of Commerce moved to block sales of advanced chips to subsidiaries of Chinese companies based outside China.

However, some of these measures have met resistance. The Semiconductor Industry Association, which represents chipmakers such as Nvidia, has opposed the Chip Security Act , saying that it cannot support “blanket mandates” for on-chip mechanisms it argues are untested and potentially infeasible.
Even if these bills pass, controls alone may not be sufficient, as Chinese firms have also sought to innovate their way around them.

One barrier Chinese companies have tried to overcome is their lack of access to advanced lithography equipment. Dutch company ASML, which makes these machines, has curbed sales to China under pressure from Washington . They are necessary for shrinking transistors, a key component of semiconductors. Adding more transistors to a chip increases its processing speed and, by extension, its computing power. In May 2026, Huawei announced a new chip-design approach that aims to increase transistor density without shrinking transistors. It hopes to match, by 2031, the transistor density of the chips Taiwan’s TSMC plans to produce in 2028 – potentially without the need for the advanced lithography machines Chinese firms struggle to obtain.

Export controls are one of the key tools the United States has used to protect its lead in AI. But Chinese firms have repeatedly sought ways to bypass them, whether through third countries or new chip designs. However the APEC summit talks go, Washington will need to remain vigilant to stay ahead.
Jack Sato
The Interpreter on United States
